pronunciation: sut-fahn
meaning: to eat; to have a meal

example.english: Have you eaten yet?

note: 「你食飯吂？」(Have you eaten?) is a classic Hakka greeting — asking whether someone has eaten is a warm way of saying hello, much like in other Chinese communities.

pronunciation: sahn-goh (like 'sahn' in 'saga' + 'go' with a flat tone)
meaning: Hakka mountain song; a traditional folk song genre

example.english: He/She can sing Hakka mountain songs.

note: Sân-kô are improvised, often antiphonal songs traditionally sung by tea pickers and farmers in the hills; they remain a proud symbol of Hakka identity and are still performed at cultural festivals in Taiwan today.

pronunciation: tee-en gong ngit (ngit rhymes with 'neat' but starts with an 'ng' sound like in 'sing')

example.english: Tomorrow I will go to school.

note: Literally 'sky-bright day' — Hakka builds time words from vivid images rather than counting units, unlike Mandarin's 明天. Compare 今晡日 (today, 'this-moment day') and 尋日 (yesterday).

pronunciation: HOKE-how (short clipped 'k', then 'how' as in cow)

example.english: He/she goes to school every day to study.

note: In older Hakka villages the 學校 was often the largest building around and doubled as a community gathering hall for meetings and festivals, not just a place for children's classes.

pronunciation: like "ngyoo" — start with the "ng" sound from "sing," then "yoo," voice dropping as you say it

example.english: The cow is eating grass.

note: Ngiù covers cows, oxen, and water buffalo alike — Hakka doesn't split them the way English does. The word shows up often in farming idioms, reflecting how central cattle were to traditional Hakka agricultural life.

pronunciation: faw-chhah (rising tone on 'faw'; 'chhah' has a puff of air on the ch, like in 'church', with a dip-then-rise tone)

example.romanization: Kì tak-ngit chhô fó-chhâ hi ho̍k-hau.
example.english: He takes the train to school every day.

note: 車 (chhâ) is the general Hakka word for wheeled vehicles, so it shows up all over transport vocabulary — 汽車 (hi-chhâ, car), 跈車 (thèn-chhâ, to ride along in a car). Old branch rail lines through Hakka hill towns like Miaoli and Neiwan made 火車 a especially everyday word in those communities.

pronunciation: m (hummed, low) — sss (rising) — kyahng
meaning: don't be afraid; no need to worry

example.english: Don't be afraid, you can do it.

note: 毋 (m̀) is Hakka's own negation word, distinct from Mandarin's 不 — 毋使 literally means 'don't need to,' so this phrase is a warm, reassuring way to calm someone rather than a blunt command.

pronunciation: sahm (rising slightly, like 'saam' but shorter)

example.english: I'm wearing this shirt.

note: In everyday Hakka, 衫 alone often just means 'clothes' in general, not just a shirt — similar to how it works in Cantonese. It's paired with the measure word 領 (liâng) for garments.

pronunciation: daw-syah (rhymes roughly with 'dough-sha', with a slight rising lift on 'sha')

example.english: Thank you for helping me.

note: Unlike Mandarin's 謝謝, Hakka speakers use 多謝 in almost every polite context, much like Cantonese 多謝 (do1 ze6) — it's the default everyday 'thanks,' not a formal or extra-emphatic one.

pronunciation: sahng-pyahng (rhymes with 'song' + 'pyang')
meaning: to become sick, to fall ill

example.romanization: Kì sâng-phiang, oi hi khon yî-sên.
example.english: He's sick, he needs to go see a doctor.

note: 生病 works as a whole verb phrase (not 'to give birth to sickness') — you can also just say 病 alone, as in 佢病忒了 (he's gotten sick), where 忒 marks a completed change of state.

pronunciation: seh (like 'set' without the t; voice drops slightly at the end)

example.english: This cookie is very small.

note: 細 also means 'young' when describing people — 細人仔 (se-ngin-é) literally means 'small person' and is the everyday Hakka word for 'child.'

pronunciation: kyoong-HEE (rhymes with 'young' + rising 'hee')
meaning: congratulations; to congratulate — the standard Lunar New Year greeting

example.english: Happy New Year, congratulations!

note: Hakka speakers often double it — 恭喜恭喜 — as a warm New Year greeting, traditionally exchanged just before elders hand out 紅包 (red envelopes) to children.

pronunciation: roughly 'suh-chong' — 市 like a clipped 'suh', 場 like 'chong' rhyming with 'song'
meaning: market (a place to buy food, produce, and daily goods)

example.english: I go to the market every day to buy vegetables.

note: Many Taiwan Hakka speakers casually borrow the Hoklo term 菜市仔 (chhài-chhī-á) for the neighborhood wet market, but 市場 is the standard Hakka word taught and used more formally.

pronunciation: lee-pie
meaning: week (also used colloquially to mean 'Sunday' when unspecified)

example.romanization: Ha lî-pai ngài oi hi Thòi-pet.
example.english: Next week I will go to Taipei.

note: 禮拜 is a loanword tied to the Western/Christian calendar that spread widely among Hakka and Hoklo speakers; unlike standard Mandarin 星期, Hakka speakers often just say 禮拜 alone to mean 'Sunday' without adding 日 or 天.

pronunciation: TAY-oo GAH (thèu rhymes with 'though', kâ like 'gah')

example.english: He is a good boss.

note: Besides 'boss', 頭家 is also a warm colloquial term a Hakka wife may use to refer to her husband, similar to how it's used in Taiwanese Hokkien — reflecting the traditional idea of the husband as household head.

pronunciation: like the "chow" in "chow mein", with a rising tone (as if asking a question)

example.english: I really like to eat fried rice.

note: 炒 shows up in one of Hakka cuisine's most famous exports, 客家小炒 (Hakka-style stir-fry) — a staple at Hakka banquets made with squid, pork, and dried tofu.

pronunciation: vawn (rising tone, like asking a question)

example.romanization: A-mê, nâ chak vón pûn ngài.
example.english: Mom, hand me a bowl.

note: The character is the same as in Mandarin, but the Hakka reading 'vón' shows the typical Hakka pattern of initial w-/hollow-sounds in Mandarin becoming v- in Hakka. 碗 is also the go-to classifier-companion word when talking about servings of rice or soup.

pronunciation: chah-cham (like 'cha' in 'chaos' + 'chum')

example.english: Where is the station?

note: 车 chhâ is the same root you already know from 火車 (fó-chhâ, train); add 站 chhâm to get 'station', and Hakka speakers often specify 火車站 (train station) vs 汽車站 (bus station).

pronunciation: say-see-en (like 'say' + 'see-en', rising then high tones)
meaning: to bathe; to take a shower/bath

example.english: I'm going to take a bath this evening.

note: Literally 'wash body' — Hakka uses 身 (body) here rather than Mandarin's 澡, so learners shouldn't try to translate word-for-word from Mandarin 洗澡.

pronunciation: TUH-oo NAH (falling tone on first syllable, level tone on second)

example.english: My head hurts.

note: 頭那 is the everyday colloquial word for 'head' in spoken Hakka, distinct from the more literary 頭 used alone in compounds like 頭家 (boss).

pronunciation: min-chong (min rhymes with 'pin', chhong rhymes with 'song' with a puff of air on 'ch')

example.english: This bed is very comfortable.

note: 眠床 literally combines '眠' (to sleep) with '床' (bed/platform), a compound retained from older Chinese that Mandarin simplified down to just 床 — Hakka keeps the fuller, more descriptive form.

pronunciation: foong-bow (rhymes with 'wow')
meaning: red envelope (gift of money given for luck)

example.hakka: 過年个時節,阿婆分𠊎紅包。
example.romanization: Go-ngièn ke sṳ̀-chiet, â-phò pûn ngài fùng-pâu.
example.english: During the Lunar New Year, grandma gives me a red envelope.

note: Red envelopes are given not only at New Year but also at weddings; the amount should avoid the number four, which sounds like 'death' and is considered unlucky.

pronunciation: soo (rising tone, like asking 'soo?')

example.english: Before eating, you must wash your hands.

note: 手 (sú) also appears in many compounds, like 手指 (sú-chṳ́, finger) — learning it early unlocks a whole family of body-part words.

pronunciation: ah-GOH

example.english: My older brother is very tall.

note: The â- prefix is added to many kinship terms in Hakka (â-gô, â-chí, â-bâ) to make them sound warm and familiar, much like adding 'my dear' — dropping it can sound blunt or distant.

pronunciation: pen-yoo (like English 'pen' + 'yoo', with the first part low and the second part rising slightly)

example.english: We are good friends.

note: The verb phrase 交朋友 (kâu phèn-yû, 'to make friends') is used the same way as in Mandarin; in Hakka villages the word is also stretched to cover friendly neighbors, not just close confidants.

pronunciation: m-SHU daw-CHA
meaning: you're welcome; no need to thank me

example.english: "Thanks for helping me." "You're welcome."

note: Literally 'no need to thank,' this is the standard polite reply after someone says 多謝 (thank you) — a natural extension for learners who already know 多謝.

pronunciation: m (a nasal hum, like saying 'hmm') + tea
meaning: "I don't know"; "dunno" — used alone as a reply, or to preface an uncertain guess

example.english: I don't know where he went.

note: Said by itself, 毋知 is a very common one-word answer (like English "dunno"), and it also shows up sentence-initially as a hedge, e.g. 毋知會毋會落雨 ("I wonder if it'll rain").

pronunciation: mook-joo (mook rhymes with 'book', joo as in 'June')

example.english: My eyes feel sore.

note: Literally 'eye-pearl' — 珠 (pearl/bead) vividly describes the round shape of the eyeball, a common pattern in Hakka body-part vocabulary.

pronunciation: ng-YONG (rhymes roughly with 'young' with a nasal ng- start)
meaning: two (used before a measure word, e.g. counting people, items, money)

example.english: This one costs two hundred dollars.

note: Like Mandarin 兩 vs 二, Hakka uses 两 (ngiông) instead of 二 (ngi) when counting things or amounts of money, while 二 is used for reading out numerals themselves (e.g. telephone numbers, page 2).

pronunciation: joh-sun (joh rhymes with 'dough' but with a hard j, sun like the star)

example.romanization: Chò-sṳ̀n, ngì sṫ pâu àn mò?
example.english: Good morning, have you eaten yet?

note: Hakka speakers often greet each other by asking whether they've eaten rather than just saying 'good morning' — the greeting 早晨 is common but pairing it with 食飽咹無 (have you eaten?) is a warm, traditional way to show care.

pronunciation: chah (like 'cha' in 'chai', falling tone)

example.english: I like drinking tea.

note: In Hakka, drinking tea uses the verb 食 (sṳ̍t, 'to eat') rather than 'drink' — the same verb used for eating rice or a meal, reflecting how central tea-drinking is treated as a meal-like activity in Hakka culture.

pronunciation: kyoh (rhymes with 'yo', rising pitch)

example.romanization: Ngài vuk-hà yû yit chak kiéu.
example.english: There is a dog at my house.

note: Notice the sound shift: many Mandarin '-ou' finals correspond to Hakka '-eu'/'-ieu' (狗 gǒu → kiéu, 走 zǒu → chéu), a handy pattern for guessing new words. The measure word 隻 (chak) is used for animals, just like Mandarin 隻/只.
